title: Who else is there?
hookLine: a demon king proposes to the Goddess; she answers with a vow, and shows that every goddess is her

lines: THE TEXT DOESN'T STOP AT THE BUFFALO.
cards: The buffalo demon is dead. You may know that story already: the gods' light pouring together into the Goddess, the lion, the shape-changing fight, her spear and sword at the end.
On the nights of Navaratri, the text that tells it, the Devi Mahatmya, is read aloud in homes and temples. And the text doesn't stop at the buffalo.
A few chapters later, two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken heaven. Their servants bring word of a beautiful woman alone in the Himalayas. And the brothers make a very bad decision.
They send her a marriage proposal.

teach.b: Shumbha's messenger arrives with the offer. The king of the three worlds wants you, he says; all the treasures of heaven are his, and they could be yours. The Goddess answers politely.
What you say is true, she tells him. But long ago I made a vow, a foolish one: whoever defeats me in battle, whoever breaks my pride, whoever is my equal in strength, he will be my husband.
So tell your king to come and win me. He goes back, and the brothers send an army.
When the generals Chanda and Munda come for her, her face darkens with anger, and from her forehead springs Kali, gaunt and terrible, who destroys them both.
So the Goddess gives Kali a name: Chamunda, the one who ended Chanda and Munda. One by one the army falls. Nishumbha falls.
At the end Shumbha, the last, shouts at her: you're proud, but you only win because others fight for you. She answers: I am alone in the world here.

teach.h: WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?
teach.b: Who else is there besides me? All the goddesses who fought beside her flow back into her body, and she faces him as one. Then she wins.

That's the teaching under the whole festival. Hindus honor many goddesses: fierce Kali, generous Lakshmi, Saraswati with her veena. In this text, they're all one Goddess, Devi, the Mother, showing different faces.
Nava, nine; ratri, night. Through these nights the text is read, many families honor a different form of her each night, and they still call her by one name: Ma.

how: During Navaratri, Hindus honor the Goddess for nine nights with fasting, prayers and songs; in Gujarat people dance garba and dandiya, in Bengal Durga Puja is celebrated, and in the south homes display rows of dolls. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, celebrates victory.

o: nine days of fasting for Shiva
nine nights kept for the Goddess
a nine-day boat race on the river

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: sent the Goddess a marriage proposal
the one who ended Chanda and Munda

s: the Devi Mahatmya ends with the buffalo demon
after the buffalo come Shumbha and Nishumbha, in the text's later chapters.
at Navaratri, Hindus worship separate goddesses who have nothing to do with each other
many honor a different form each night, but in the Devi Mahatmya every goddess flows back into the one Devi.
Shumbha says she wins only because others fight for her
so she draws every goddess back into herself: who else is there besides me?

games.q: the last demon king sneers: you only win because other goddesses fight for you. what does the Goddess do?
o: call even more goddesses to help her.
draw every goddess back into herself, and face him alone.
agree, and let the others finish the fight.
games.why: they all flow back into her: who else is there besides me? every goddess was one Goddess all along.

practice: Through Navaratri many Hindus light a small lamp before the Goddess each night and call her Ma. If you pray, light one, or picture one, and say a few of her names slowly: Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kali.
Notice how different they feel, fierce, generous, wise, wild, and hold them as one face. If you don't pray, think of someone you know who is many things at once, and still one person.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights of the Goddess, and a tenth day of victory.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Chamunda, the name the Goddess gives Kali after Chanda and Munda fall.

carryVoice: Your line: one goddess, many forms. Who else is there besides me? Every name is hers. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana 81–93), chapters 5–10 (Shumbha and Nishumbha; the Goddess's vow; Kali and the name Chamunda; the goddesses drawn back into one)
Navaratri observance (garba, Durga Puja, golu, Vijayadashami)
